docs.title: 6 formulas
docs.text:
\[\text{PPV} = \frac{\text{sens}\cdot p}{\text{sens}\cdot p + (1-\text{spec})(1-p)} \qquad \text{NPV} = \frac{\text{spec}(1-p)}{\text{spec}(1-p)+(1-\text{sens})p}\] \[O/E = \frac{\text{observed deaths}}{\text{mean predicted risk}\times n}\]
  • \(TP=\text{sens}\times P\), \(FN=(1-\text{sens})P\), \(FP=(1-\text{spec})N\), \(TN=\text{spec}\cdot N\).
  • Calibration = predicted vs observed; discrimination = AUROC. O/E needs calibration.
  • Softmax over \(k\) candidates: a score is relative, not a calibrated probability.
  • Mean of readings loses trend: keep slope, min, max, last value.

docs.title: 6 open-question templates
docs.text:
1. "Lower loss but worse facts" → loss averages over common tokens; teacher forcing vs own output; evaluate rare critical facts with blinded clinicians.
  2. "Novel perturbation/drug" → categorical embedding cannot extrapolate; need structure/feature encoder or graph prior.
  3. "Biased/leaky evaluation" → say the specific leakage (future data, patient overlap, balancing, treatment paradox), then the fix (causal inputs, patient-level temporal split, real prevalence, exclude treated negatives).
  4. "Deployment decision" → intended use → unit of output → local validation → operating point (who bears FP vs FN) → monitoring + exit plan → economics.
  5. "Workflow or agent?" → can the paths be enumerated in advance? Yes → workflow; no → agent/orchestrator. Not "does it use an LLM".
  6. "Evaluate an LLM system" → build a test set with injected errors/missing data; measure outcome, process (evidence attribution, unnecessary steps) and cost; distinguish supported from accidentally correct.

docs.title: 5 rules that earn points
docs.text:
1. Name the mechanism, then the consequence. "Attention is permutation-equivariant, therefore both reports give the same averaged vector."
  2. Always separate discrimination from calibration. AUROC is threshold-free; decisions need a threshold and calibration.
  3. Say whose error it is. False positive vs false negative, and who signs off.
  4. State what a result cannot establish. One split, one site, no CIs → no significance, no transportability.
  5. For any model claim, ask: was the reference standard independent of the model? Anchoring and "zero discrepancies" are not validation.

docs.title: The one-line answer to most essay questions
docs.text: The model's score is only a ranking; the clinical decision needs an operating point, calibration, validation on the local case mix, and a named owner for the residual risk.

Multiple choice · answer key
docs.text:
20% of the grade15 minLearn the traps

All Mentimeter questions from lectures 1–2 and 6, with the correct option and the one-line reason. The percentages are what the class voted — where the majority was wrong, that is the trap.

docs.title: Lectures 1–2
1. In autoregressive pretraining, where do the targets come from?
docs.text:
✅ Each observed token serves as the target following its preceding context. (83%)

The text supplies its own labels; no annotator. The "own generated continuation" option is wrong — that would be self-training, not pretraining. Masked-token prediction is BERT-style, not autoregressive.

docs.title: 2. In \(h_i^{(0)} = e(x_i) + p_i\), what is \(p_i\)?
docs.text:
✅ The position of the token in the sequence. (87%)

An embedding of the index, added so the model can distinguish the same token at different locations.

docs.title: 3. What defines self-attention vs cross-attention?
docs.text:
✅ Queries, keys and values come from the same input sequence. (59%)

Cross-attention takes queries from one sequence (e.g. decoder) and keys/values from another (e.g. encoder). Same projection matrix is not required.

docs.title: 4. Zero-shot vs few-shot prompting?
docs.text:
✅ Zero-shot supplies no task demonstrations; few-shot supplies examples. (45%)

Both keep the weights frozen. "Uses no pretrained knowledge" is the trap: zero-shot still relies on pretraining.

docs.title: 5. LoRA shapes for \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times k}\), \(\Delta W = BA\) of rank \(r\)?
docs.text:
✅ \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\) and \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{r\times k}\). (90%)

Inner dimensions \(r\) must match; the product gives \(d\times k\).

docs.title: 6. Why use different augmented views in visual self-supervision?
docs.text:
✅ They provide related observations from which to learn consistent representations. (83%)

Invariance learning. They do not preserve every clinical detail (augmentation can destroy some) and do not replace an objective.

docs.title: 7. Purpose of a contrastive image–text objective?
docs.text:
✅ Matching pairs get higher similarity than mismatched pairs. (72%)

It is not caption generation, pixel reconstruction, nor independent classification.

docs.title: 8. Image-to-report retrieval vs report generation?
docs.text: ✅ Retrieval selects an existing report; generation predicts a sequence of tokens. (93%)

docs.title: 9. Linear probe \(p = \text{softmax}(Wz + b)\) with fixed \(z = f_\theta(x)\): what is fitted?
docs.text:
✅ \(W\) and \(b\); \(\theta\) is fixed. (58%)

That is the definition of a linear probe.

docs.title: 10. External validation?
docs.text:
✅ Evaluation on independently collected data from outside the development source. (93%)

A random held-out subset of the same dataset is internal validation.

docs.title: Lecture 6
11. In ReAct, where does the observation after a search come from?
docs.text:
✅ The search tool executed by the surrounding program. (36%)

The model requests; the environment executes and returns text. The tool description in the prompt is the trap (41% voted for it).

docs.title: 12. Which description captures ReAct?
docs.text:
✅ Interleave reasoning and actions, using observations to inform subsequent steps. (83%)

Not a plan fixed in advance, not a post-hoc explanation, not two separate trained models.

docs.title: 13. How do few-shot demonstrations influence a ReAct model?
docs.text:
✅ They provide example trajectories in the context while weights stay fixed. (73%)

In-context learning. They do not update parameters or train a controller.

docs.title: 14. Why can external search reduce factual hallucinations?
docs.text:
✅ It supplies evidence the model can use in subsequent reasoning. (100%)

It does not update weights after each search.

docs.title: 15. Main distinction between workflows and agents?
docs.text:
✅ Workflows use predefined code paths; agents let the LLM direct the process and tool use. (74%)

22% picked "workflows keep weights fixed, agents update them" — wrong: neither updates weights.

docs.title: 16. Extract findings → draft summary → translate. Which pattern?
docs.text:
✅ Prompt chaining. (100%)

Sequential LLM calls, each consuming the previous output.

docs.title: 17. Classify a request and send it to one of several specialist handlers?
docs.text:
✅ Routing.

The class voted 100% for parallelization, which is the trap. Parallelization runs independent subtasks and aggregates; routing selects one path. This is the single most likely MCQ trap to reappear.

docs.title: 18. Which capability is least tested by a static medical MCQ benchmark?
docs.text:
✅ Deciding what information to request as a consultation develops. (84%)

Static questions test recall and single-step association; they cannot test interactive information gathering.

docs.title: 19. Role of agent-based modelling in the proposed clinical evaluations?
docs.text:
✅ To simulate the actions and interactions of participants in a clinical environment.

Not to replace the encounter with one fixed Q&A, not to train the next-token predictor, not to rank models by size/speed.

docs.title: 20. An agent performs well in a clinical simulation. What next?
docs.text:
✅ Test real-world impact in clinical studies and monitor after deployment. (90%)

More simulation runs or more static questions do not address transfer.

docs.title: Traps to remember
docs.text: Tempting option Why it is wrong Workflows train/update weights Both workflows and agents keep weights fixed Parallelization for a router Routing selects one path; parallelization runs all Tool description = observation The program executes the tool; the description is only instructions Few-shot = fine-tuning Demonstrations are in context; weights unchanged Zero-shot = no pretrained knowledge It uses pretraining, just no demonstrations Retrieval generates reports Retrieval selects an existing report Balanced test set gives real precision Precision depends on prevalence 0.90 softmax = 90% disease probability Softmax is relative to the candidate set AUROC 0.97 settles the threshold AUROC is threshold-free; the operating point is a clinical decision

docs.title: Lecture 1 · Language models
Problem 1 — Lower loss, more factual errors
docs.text:
A model drafts patient letters. A has lower average next-token loss than B, but more often writes "normal" when the report says "pending".

Answer.

  1. Next-token loss is an average over all tokens, and most tokens are shared boilerplate. Result statements are rare and have several plausible wordings, so errors there barely move the average. Loss is also measured with teacher forcing (the reference prefix is given), while generation feeds the model its own output, so errors compound (exposure bias). A lower average loss only establishes that A assigns slightly higher likelihood to observed tokens on average under teacher forcing — it says nothing about factual consistency on the clinically important, rare tokens.
  2. Greedy decoding does not solve it. The problem is in the learned distribution and the evaluation target, not the sampling. Greedy can even make it worse: the most probable continuation after "Result" may be the frequent phrase "was normal", and greedy removes the chance of sampling the correct rare token. It can also produce degenerate repetition.
  3. Clinician assessment: sample held-out reports stratified to include pending results, abnormal values and rare findings, not just the common ones. Each clinician sees the source report and the two generated letters in random order, blinded to which model produced which (or rates them independently). They mark every factual claim as supported / contradicted / unsupported, plus a severity. Primary outcome: proportion of letters with at least one clinically significant factual error; secondary: errors per letter. Compare paired by report (McNemar), report confidence intervals, and measure inter-rater agreement. This controls for report difficulty.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Position vectors before vs after the Transformer
docs.text:
Reports: left opacity right clear → left; left clear right opacity → right. Architecture A adds position vectors before the Transformer, B after.

Answer.

  • A works. Positions are injected at the input, so every token embedding already carries "which side am I on". Attention compares content and position jointly, and the classifier receives an averaged representation in which the opacity token is tagged left or right. The two reports produce different averaged vectors.
  • B fails. Without positional information, self-attention is permutation-equivariant: it sees the same multiset of token embeddings for both reports. Adding position vectors after the Transformer only adds the same fixed pattern to both, and the average over positions is identical for both inputs (\(\frac14\sum_i h_i + \frac14\sum_i p_i\)). The classifier gets exactly the same vector, so it cannot distinguish left from right.
  • General point: positional information must enter before any operation that mixes tokens; averaging afterwards cannot recover an order that was never encoded.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Causal mask only in layer 2
docs.text:
Tokens finding → is → absent. Layer 1 is full attention, layer 2 is causal. Claim: at "is", layer 2 cannot use "absent".

Answer. The claim is wrong. The causal mask in layer 2 only restricts attention within layer 2. The input to layer 2 at position "is" is the layer-1 output, and layer 1 attended to all positions, including "absent". So the representation of "is" already contains information about "absent" before the mask is applied. The model can predict "absent" from a representation that has seen the answer — target leakage. Masking must be causal from the first layer (or at every layer) for a decoder-only model to be valid.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Guidelines that change several times per year
docs.text:
Answer. Use retrieval-augmented generation, not fine-tuning on history. Index the current guidelines with document ID, section and version. At request time, use the patient characteristics to retrieve the applicable sections, put them in the prompt with their version metadata, and require the answer to cite the supporting document and version (or abstain if nothing relevant is retrieved). Re-index when guidelines change; the model weights never need to change.

Fine-tuning on historical examples is insufficient because the guidelines change several times a year (the weights encode a frozen snapshot and cannot cite a version), rare patient groups are underrepresented so the model cannot learn their rules, and fine-tuning does not prevent confident hallucination.

A way the system can still fail: retrieval selects the wrong or an outdated section (bad chunking, embedding miss, version not filtered), the prompt contains conflicting sections, or the patient characteristics used for retrieval are incomplete, so the model produces a recommendation that is correctly cited but not applicable. Mitigation: version filtering, multiple retrievals, and abstain when no passage matches.

docs.title: Problem 5 — LoRA adapters: per department vs pooled
docs.text:
Per-department adapters give 90/90/90; pooled gives 94/82/80 (A has 800 eval letters, B and C only 100 each).

Answer.

  1. Do not adopt pooled on the aggregate number alone. The aggregate is dominated by department A (800 of 1000 letters), and this is a Simpson-style aggregation: pooling helps A but costs B and C eight to ten points — a large, clinically relevant regression in exactly the departments with less data. Next action: report results stratified by department with confidence intervals, test whether B/C drops are significant, inspect the errors (does pooled ignore departmental instruction style?), and require no subgroup degradation as an acceptance criterion. Then decide between per-department adapters or a pooled adapter plus department-specific adapters.
  2. LoRA keeps the base weights frozen and learns a low-rank update \(\Delta W = BA\) per layer. Store one copy of the base model plus three small adapter sets and swap/route by department at inference (multi-adapter serving); memory is shared, and only the adapters differ.

docs.title: Lecture 2 · Vision models
Problem 1 — Teacher momentum \(m\)
docs.text:
Answer.

  • \(m=0\): the teacher is replaced by the student after every step. There is no stable target; the teacher chases the student and the objective can collapse or oscillate.
  • \(m=0.9\): an exponential moving average with a horizon of about 10 steps. The teacher follows quickly, giving only mild stability.
  • \(m=0.999\): horizon about 1000 steps. The teacher changes slowly, providing consistent targets and preventing a fast student–teacher feedback loop that collapses representations. This is the useful regime.
  • \(m=1\): the teacher is frozen at initialisation. It is stable but useless — the student is trained to match random/initial features, which encodes no knowledge.

A slowly changing teacher is useful because it acts like an ensemble of past student checkpoints, giving stable, low-variance targets that avoid collapse and make self-supervised learning work without labels.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Removing feature-spread regularisation from DINOv2
docs.text:
Answer. Without the spread regulariser (KoLeo-style), the matching objective can be satisfied by mapping many images/patches into a narrow region of feature space: dimensional collapse / feature crowding. Local neighbours become uninformative even if global collapse is prevented by centering and sharpening. Patch features in particular lose the diversity needed for segmentation and dense tasks.

Compare between runs: the effective rank / singular-value spectrum of the feature matrix, the distribution of pairwise distances (and kNN distance), linear-probe accuracy on image-level labels, patch-level segmentation/dense probes, clustering quality, and attention-map diversity. Matching loss alone is not sufficient: it can be low while features are collapsed or uniformly spread without semantic structure; you need downstream probes and spread diagnostics.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Frozen linear probe vs fine-tuning
docs.text:
Encoder A: 78% frozen, 86% fine-tuned. Encoder B: 84% frozen, 85% fine-tuned.

Answer. Frozen + linear head favours B (84 vs 78). Fine-tuning favours A (86 vs 85). The rankings differ because a linear probe only measures how linearly separable the existing features are, whereas fine-tuning can reshape the representation; A's features may be less linearly accessible but more adaptable (better initialisation for the task), while B may already be near its ceiling.

The table alone cannot establish: whether the differences are statistically significant (one split, no CIs), whether they hold on external data or other tasks, whether A's fine-tuned gain is overfitting, or the cost/compute difference. A single 1-point gap is well within noise.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Softmax scores and a third description
docs.text: Answer. Yes, the score for "abnormal" can change even if its similarity is unchanged, because softmax normalises over the candidate set: adding "pneumonia" changes the denominator and takes probability mass from every existing option. The 0.90 is a relative score within the prompt set, not a calibrated probability of disease. Reporting it as a patient probability is misleading; you would need calibration on held-out data for a fixed, clinically defined candidate set.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Two identical captions in a CLIP batch
docs.text:
Answer. No. Both images have the same positive text vector, so for image 1 the two identical texts are indistinguishable in the softmax: it cannot assign all probability to its own copy while assigning none to the other, because their similarities are equal. The best it can do is split the mass between them (e.g. 0.5/0.5), and gradients from the two rows conflict.

Fix: deduplicate the batch, or use a contrastive objective that treats all identical texts as positives (multiple-positive / debiased contrastive loss), or construct batches so that no two texts are identical.

docs.title: Problem 6 — CLIP vector into a frozen text-only LM
docs.text:
Answer. Search: using frozen CLIP for text–image retrieval is reasonable zero-shot, but validate on the archive (domain shift, prompt wording, threshold).

Explanations: matching the vector length is not enough. The CLIP embedding lives in a different space, with a different scale and distribution, from the LM's token embeddings; the LM has never learned to interpret it, so it is out-of-distribution and the model will ignore or misread it. You need a learned projection (linear/MLP) mapping image features into the LM embedding space, trained on image–text pairs, plus instruction tuning so the LM learns to use visual tokens. Often the image is mapped to several tokens, not one.

docs.title: Problem 7 — Small head on frozen encoder vs instruction-tuned VLM
docs.text:
Answer.

  • A (frozen encoder + small head): cheap, fast, deterministic, easy to calibrate, monitor and validate; needs representative labels; cannot explain or handle new questions.
  • B (instruction-tuned VLM): flexible, can explain and follow new instructions, no new labels; but expensive, slower, prompt-sensitive, harder to calibrate, more failure modes, harder to audit.

If both meet accuracy, choose on cost/latency at the fixed inference budget, calibration (ECE), per-class recall, robustness to shift, stability across prompt wording, and auditability. Additional measurements: external validation set, subgroup performance, calibration curve, inference cost per image, and error severity analysis.

docs.title: Bonus B1 — Adding "ultrasound" to a frozen CLIP classifier
docs.text: Answer. Add the text description(s) for ultrasound; CLIP compares the image embedding with the new text embedding, so no retraining is required to produce a prediction. What must be checked: that ultrasound images are actually closer to the ultrasound prompt than to X-ray/CT/MRI prompts (validate on labelled ultrasound images), prompt wording, confusion with other modalities, and that thresholds/calibration still hold. Zero-shot performance for a new class is not guaranteed just because the class was added.

docs.title: Bonus B2 — More captions vs specific question–answer pairs
docs.text: Answer. Specific question–answer pairs address the behaviour more directly: they teach instruction following and question-conditioned answering, which caption alignment does not. More image–caption pairs only improve broad descriptive alignment. Limitation of the QA option: it does not by itself fix hallucination or factual grounding, and it may not generalise to questions outside the collected distribution.

docs.title: Bonus B3 — Retrieval-augmented visual assistant
docs.text: Answer. Design a within-image, paired comparison: the same assistant with and without retrieved captions, on the same held-out images, stratified by radiologist-rated difficulty. Radiologists are blinded to condition and assess factual correctness, completeness, hallucinated findings, and whether the output is influenced by captions that do not match the image. To separate useful context from retrieved-caption errors: check whether claims match the retrieved captions but not the image (attribution/overlap analysis), and include a condition with deliberately wrong retrieved captions to see whether the assistant copies them. Keep retrieval only if it improves accuracy on difficult images without increasing caption-induced errors.

docs.title: Lecture 3 · Omics models
Problem 1 — How scVI addresses five challenges
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. Sparsity / excess zeros — zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) likelihood: a dropout gate models excess zeros, the NB component models counts and overdispersion.
  2. Varying sequencing depth — the observed library size \(l_i\) enters the NB mean as an explicit scaling factor, so the latent representation is normalised for depth.
  3. Batch effects — batch is a categorical covariate fed to the encoder and decoder (conditional VAE), so the model learns batch-specific parameters while \(z\) captures biology.
  4. Biological/transcriptional noise — a probabilistic latent variable with a prior (VAE), sampled stochastically, plus NB dispersion; inference is amortised rather than per-cell.
  5. Scalability — amortised variational inference with an encoder network + mini-batch SGD on GPU, instead of optimising per-cell parameters.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Genes as a sentence
docs.text:
Answer. scRNA-seq is a set of genes with expression values, not an ordered sequence: gene order is arbitrary, so positional embeddings are meaningless, and the list length/set varies per cell. Feeding gene identity alone also discards the expression magnitude and the zero pattern.

Two changes: (1) embed gene identity + expression value (e.g. \(h_i = \text{emb}_g(g_i) + \text{emb}_x(x_i)\), with values normalised/log-transformed); (2) make the architecture order-invariant (no positional embeddings; set-transformer/attention without position, or rank-based ordering), and normalise for library size.

docs.title: Problem 3 — TP53 in two cells
docs.text: Answer. Initial embedding: identical, because the gene identity and expression value are the same. Post-Transformer: different, because self-attention mixes TP53 with the other genes expressed in that cell; in a stressed cancer cell the co-expressed context (stress, proliferation, immune programmes) differs, so TP53's contextualised representation changes. That is the biological capability: a gene's representation becomes context-dependent, capturing gene–gene interactions and cell state rather than a fixed dictionary meaning.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Zero-shot foundation model vs scVI on a new dataset
docs.text:
Answer. Based on Kedzierska et al., expect the dataset-fitted model (scVI) to integrate the batches better and often preserve biological variation better than zero-shot foundation-model embeddings, which were not trained on this dataset and tend to carry batch structure. Zero-shot embeddings are convenient but not automatically better.

If batch is strongly confounded with biology (cancer vs normal in different batches), aggressive batch integration can remove the biological signal it is supposed to preserve. Then a zero-shot representation that has not been optimised to remove this dataset's batch effect may retain more biology and could be preferable — at the cost of leaving batch structure in. The right response is to evaluate both on biological conservation metrics (e.g. cell-type separation, marker recovery), not to assume integration is always good.

docs.title: Problem 5 — CPA and a novel drug
docs.text:
Answer. Standard CPA represents each perturbation by a learned embedding, so a drug never seen in training has no embedding and cannot be predicted zero-shot. To generalise you need a perturbation representation that transfers to unseen drugs (chemical structure/fingerprint encoder, or a model trained on mechanism classes).

If the adversarial perturbation discriminator weight is zero, the basal state \(z_\text{basal}\) is no longer forced to be perturbation-invariant: it can absorb perturbation information, so the model stops cleanly separating "cell state" from "drug effect". Counterfactual predictions for unseen drug combinations then become unreliable, because the decomposition that makes them meaningful is no longer enforced.

docs.title: Problem 6 — Why GEARS needs \(G_\text{pert}\)
docs.text:
Answer. \(G_\text{gene}\) encodes gene co-expression: which genes are expressed together. \(G_\text{pert}\) encodes similarity between perturbations: which perturbations have similar downstream effects (e.g. same pathway/complex). GEARS propagates information over \(G_\text{pert}\) so that the embedding of an unobserved knockout can be inferred from perturbations with similar effects.

If you use \(G_\text{gene}\) for perturbation message passing, you relate perturbations through gene co-expression, which is not the same relationship; a never-perturbed gene cannot borrow strength from biologically similar perturbations, so zero-shot prediction of its knockout effect collapses to something like an average or is arbitrary.

docs.title: Problem 7 — Low global MSE with a No-Change baseline
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. About 50 of 10,000 genes change per treatment, so predicting the control state is correct for ~99.5% of entries; the global MSE is dominated by the vast unchanged majority.
  2. The neural network can achieve a low global MSE by predicting close to control almost everywhere; its errors on the few changed genes contribute almost nothing to the average, so global MSE hides whether it learned treatment-specific effects. The improvement 0.06 → 0.05 may be clinically irrelevant.
  3. Evaluate only on differentially expressed genes (top-k by effect size), use per-gene standardised errors or delta/correlation metrics (predicted vs observed effect sizes), report MSE on changed genes separately, and use ranking metrics. Feature selection should focus on genes with real treatment effects rather than all 10,000.

docs.title: Lecture 4 · Models for hospital data
Problem 1 — Aggregation destroys information
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. No difference: both patients have mean systolic pressure 100 mmHg, so the row is identical; the trend (recovering vs deteriorating) is lost.
  2. The ten chunk embeddings are averaged, so the one chunk with "new pleural effusion" contributes 1/10 of the text vector; mean pooling dilutes sparse but critical findings, and a chunk-level clinical embedding may not preserve the detail/negation strongly enough.
  3. Vital signs: keep trend features (slope, min, max, last value, time since abnormal) instead of only the mean — new problem: more features, collinearity and missingness, higher overfitting risk. Text: keep per-chunk embeddings or use attention/max pooling, or retrieve salient sentences — new problem: much higher dimensionality, more data needed, and attention weights are harder to interpret/validate.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Metrics under class balancing
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. Sensitivity, specificity and AUROC can carry over, because they are conditional on the true class (or threshold-free) and do not depend on prevalence. Precision and accuracy cannot: they depend on the prevalence, which was changed by undersampling.
  2. At 10% prevalence: \(\text{PPV} = \frac{0.7 \times 0.1}{0.7 \times 0.1 + 0.3 \times 0.9} = \frac{0.07}{0.34} \approx 0.21\). So about 2 in 10 alarms, not 7.
  3. Build the test set with the real prevalence (no undersampling; if you must balance for training, reweight or recalibrate for evaluation). Ask additionally for a calibration curve, decision-curve/net benefit, and external validation at another site.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Treatment paradox in septic shock labels
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. A fluid bolus is given because of early signs of sepsis. Treated patients who never develop shock are labelled negative, so the model learns "bolus → low risk". Patients who resemble those treated negatives then get underestimated risk — confounding by indication / treatment paradox.
  2. Removing all bolus patients fixes that bias but creates selection bias: you remove a clinically important subgroup, change the case mix, and the model is no longer applicable to the patients most likely to be treated; you also lose information about the effect of treatment.
  3. Treated patients who never developed shock are "cured" by the intervention: including them in evaluation would count the treatment's success (or the model's missed opportunity) as model performance. Excluding them makes the reported performance apply only to untreated/selected patients; it does not tell you how the model performs in the full deployed population, and it cannot estimate the causal effect of the alert.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Bidirectional LSTM reused for hourly alerts
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. For the 24-hour mortality model, the prediction is made at hour 24 using the completed 24-hour window, so reading forwards and backwards uses no information from after the prediction time. Bidirectionality is acceptable.
  2. No, "dataset shift" is not sufficient. At hour \(t\) the bidirectional network reads the whole stay, including future hours: retrospective AUROC is inflated by future information leakage. Other causes: retrospective vs prospective differences in data capture, missingness, alert-response behaviour, case mix, and clinician workflow changes.
  3. Feed causal inputs: truncate the sequence at each prediction hour and use a causal/unidirectional model, or train on snapshots with only data available at that hour. Evaluate retrospectively on hourly snapshots (predict at \(t\), label \(t\) to \(t+12\)), excluding post-event data, and simulate deployment conditions; then a prospective silent trial.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Discrimination vs calibration for ICU comparison
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. AUROC favours A (0.91 vs 0.88): better discrimination. Average predicted risk favours B for calibration (8.5% vs observed 8%; A predicts 19%, overestimating). In the 30–40% band, A predicts 12% observed (overestimates) while B's 33% is close. So A ranks better, B is calibrated better.
  2. 200 patients × 8% = 16 deaths. Model A predicts 19% × 200 = 38 deaths. O/E = 16/38 ≈ 0.42, suggesting this ICU performs much better than expected — or, more likely, that model A overestimates risk.
  3. Use B (or recalibrate A on held-out data with Platt/isotonic scaling) for O/E comparison, because O/E requires calibration. The table alone cannot establish whether O/E differences reflect quality of care vs case-mix differences (risk adjustment), statistical uncertainty, or subgroup calibration.

docs.title: Problem 6 — Adding X-rays: 0.90 on a selected 1,500
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. Not justified. The 0.90 is measured only in the 1,500 patients who had a chest X-ray in the first 24 hours, and those patients have 14% mortality vs 7% overall — a sicker, selected group. The +0.04 cannot be attributed to X-rays for all patients; it is confounded by indication/selection.
  2. At hospital K: no free-text notes, so the notes path is unavailable (structured-only performance, ~0.86 or worse); every ICU patient has an admission X-ray, but the model was trained on selected X-ray patients, so applying the X-ray path to everyone is a different distribution. Expect a performance drop and calibration shift, plus different missing-modality behaviour.
  3. Before use: external validation at K, stratified by available modality, calibration, robustness to missing notes, case-mix comparison, and a prospective silent trial with monitoring.

docs.title: Problem 7 — Age and false-positive rates
docs.text:
Answer.

  1. Older patients have higher baseline mortality and comorbidity, so a fixed threshold flags more of them; age is a strong predictor correlated with frailty and atypical presentation. The higher FPR may partly reflect genuine risk, but the disparity is still a fairness problem.
  2. Removing age is unlikely to fix it: the model can reconstruct age from proxies (diagnoses, labs, procedures, notes), so the disparity persists while performance drops and the model becomes less transparent. It treats a symptom, not the cause.
  3. Alternative: subgroup-aware calibration / equalised-odds post-processing, reweighting or more training data for older groups, and auditing subgroup calibration and net benefit. Measure FPR/TPR by group, calibration curves, and clinical net benefit; involve clinicians in setting acceptable trade-offs.

docs.title: Bonus B1 — Random split vs temporal + patient split
docs.text: Answer. Team 2's 0.81 is the better estimate of live performance in 2027. Two separate reasons for the gap: (1) Team 1's random split leaks patients across splits — repeat admissions of the same patient appear in train and test — and ignores time; (2) Team 2's split reflects temporal drift and future deployment, and excludes patients seen in training. Before going live: calibration, subgroup performance, monitoring/drift plan, and consistency of the data pipeline.

docs.title: Bonus B2 — Missing lactate and a new protocol
docs.text:
Answer. The "was measured" feature is a proxy for clinician concern, which is legitimate information available at prediction time — but it is fragile: it encodes a workflow decision, not physiology. After the protocol, lactate is measured for everyone, so the feature becomes constant and loses its predictive power; the lactate distribution also shifts (more normal values), breaking the learned association. Expect miscalibration and a performance drop.

Handling: monitor and retrain/recalibrate after the protocol change, version the model, and replace workflow-artefact features with explicit clinical-concern variables if possible; validate prospectively before relying on it.

docs.title: Lecture 6 · Agentic AI
Problem 1 — Tool description in the prompt
docs.text: Answer. No. Describing the tool only makes the model able to produce a correctly formatted request; it does not establish that the request is executed, that arguments are valid, that the result is parsed and fed back, or that the tool behaves correctly on real inputs. You need an end-to-end test: actual invocation, schema validation, failure/error handling, and evaluation of final outputs against ground truth across representative cases.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Predefined workflow vs agent
docs.text: Answer. Choose the predefined workflow. The possible paths are known in advance: quality fail → replace; incomplete measurements → human review. The deciding question is whether the possible paths can be enumerated, not whether the system branches or uses an LLM. An agent adds non-determinism, cost, latency and validation burden with no benefit when the decision logic is fixed. A workflow with explicit branches and human-review steps is easier to validate, monitor and audit.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Parallelization vs orchestrator-workers
docs.text: Answer. A → predefined parallelization: the three summaries are independent and defined before execution. B → orchestrator-workers: which reviews/analyses are relevant depends on the case, so decomposition must happen at runtime. The architectural difference that matters is whether subtasks are fixed in advance or chosen by the orchestrator. Orchestration adds coordination cost: extra LLM calls and latency, error propagation, non-determinism, harder evaluation, and a synthesizer that must reconcile outputs — justified only when the task genuinely cannot be decomposed in advance.

docs.title: Problem 4 — Evaluator–optimizer criteria
docs.text:
Answer. Direct checks against source records (deterministic): every requested finding present; values and units preserved exactly; chronology/order correct; no fabricated values. Judgement of text (needs a judge): clarity, clinical coherence, no unsupported claims, appropriate emphasis.

Accept only when all deterministic checks pass and the judge scores above a threshold with no new unsupported claims. Use a revision limit as a fallback, but record "revision limit reached" as a failure, distinct from acceptance; log the acceptance reason. Beware evaluator drift and self-preference, so keep a held-out human-rated set to validate the evaluator itself.

docs.title: Problem 5 — AI-SCE-style evaluation of workflow vs agent
docs.text:
Answer. Include situations with missing information, inconsistent records (conflicting medications/labs), ambiguous findings, and routine controls. Record every tool call, query, step taken, tokens/time, and whether missing information was identified and inconsistencies resolved. Compare outcomes (correctness/completeness vs ground truth), process quality (evidence attribution, unnecessary queries, appropriate escalation), and resource use (calls, latency, cost).

To distinguish a well-supported summary from an accidentally correct one: require each statement to cite its source record, score unsupported-but-correct statements as failures, and inject known inconsistencies so you can check detection. Use paired cases and blinded graders.

docs.title: Pattern summary
docs.text: If the question says… Reach for… "lower loss but worse facts" teacher forcing vs generation, loss dominated by common tokens, evaluate the rare critical facts "position added before/after" permutation equivariance; positional info must enter before mixing; averaging destroys order "mask in layer 2 only" leakage through earlier full-attention layer; masking must be causal everywhere "guidelines change / cite the source" RAG + versioned index + citation/abstain, not fine-tuning "per-group vs pooled" stratified metrics, Simpson-style aggregation, subgroup regression "momentum / EMA teacher" stability vs plasticity; slow teacher avoids collapse "frozen probe vs fine-tune" linear separability vs adaptability; a single split cannot establish significance "softmax over descriptions" relative score, not calibrated probability "identical texts in batch" contrastive conflict, multiple positives / dedup "vector length matches" projection + alignment training needed "unseen drug / unperturbed gene" categorical perturbation embedding cannot extrapolate; graph prior transfers "global MSE low" dominated by unchanged genes; evaluate DE genes/deltas "mean of readings" trend information lost; keep slope/min/max "balanced test set, 10% prevalence" PPV = sens·prev / (sens·prev + (1−spec)(1−prev)) "AUROC 0.95 retrospective, 0.71 live" future leakage, not just dataset shift "O/E comparison between ICUs" needs calibration, not just AUROC; risk adjustment "remove age to be fair" proxies remain; subgroup calibration/equalised odds "tool described in prompt" description ≠ execution; end-to-end test "all exceptions known" workflow, not agent "subtasks fixed vs case-dependent" parallelization vs orchestrator-workers

Clinical workflow cases · worked answers
docs.text:
Lecture 58 deployment casesThe 50% part

The eight guided self-study cases from "Integration of AI in the clinical workflow". Each answer follows the required structure: the decision, the number that drove it, the risk you cannot mitigate, and who owns that risk.

Exam move

For any deployment scenario, answer in this order: intended use → unit of output → validation → operating point → monitoring/exit plan → economics. Most lost points come from jumping to AUROC before asking whether the use is even inside the intended use.

docs.title: Case 1 — Melanoma model meets dermatopathology
docs.text:
Published research model, AUROC 0.96 on 1,200 curated balanced slides from one scanner; web app; 14,000 skin specimens/year; melanocytic lesions 18%, re-excisions 7%.

Scope. Melanocytic lesions: \(0.18 \times 14{,}000 = 2{,}520\) specimens/year, and at ~3 slides each ≈ 7,560 slides/year. The other 82% (BCC, SCC/AK, seborrhoeic keratosis, inflammatory, re-excisions, other) are out of scope: the model has no validated output for them. Routing is decided at accessioning/triage by the lab, not by the model.

Unit of output. One probability per slide is not a diagnosis. The report needs: lesion classification with subtype, Bresenham thickness, ulceration, mitotic rate, margin status (peripheral/deep), lymphovascular invasion, regression, and a case-level integrated diagnosis across slides. The model gives none of these, and no uncertainty or evidence per feature.

Allowed? No, as it stands. Governance problems: (1) it is a research prototype, not CE-IVD/MDR-certified, with no intended-use statement; (2) sending patient slides to an external university web app needs a data-processing agreement, GDPR basis, and security review; (3) no local validation on your scanner, population and case mix; (4) no accreditation/quality system, monitoring or liability agreement. Local validation alone would not fix the regulatory status.

docs.title: Case 2 — One prostate model, three proposals
docs.text:
CE-IVD, intended use: adjunct, pathologist reviews all slides. 12 cores on 6 slides, 3-week backlog.

  • A — worklist prioritisation: inside intended use. Every case is still read; this only changes order. Validation duty: show that prioritisation does not delay the rest beyond an acceptable bound.
  • B — in-viewer overlay: inside intended use (adjunct, pathologist reviews everything). Validation: overlay does not cause misses/automation bias.
  • C — "AI benign" fast track: outside intended use. It converts an adjunct into a rule-out/sign-out tool, which is a new clinical claim: new validation, potentially new regulatory status, and new liability. It also requires a case-level operating point and a documented policy for who signs out.

Aggregation. For A, use the maximum slide score per case — you want suspicious cases first, so any positive core should raise the case. For C, the case is "AI benign" only if every slide (and every core) has \(p < \tau\), i.e. the case score is the max; using the mean would dilute one positive core and destroy case-level sensitivity.

Tomorrow's choice. Take A, with one condition: a prospective audit of time-to-read for high-score cases and a monthly review of misses in the prioritised list; no case may be delayed beyond the agreed window.

docs.title: Case 3 — Choose the operating point
docs.text:
10,000 node slides/year (250 working days = 40/day), 5% metastasis → 500 positive, 9,500 negative.

Sens Spec TP FP FN TN PPV NPV Flags/day A 0.99 0.70 495 2,850 5 6,650 14.8% 99.92% 13.4 B 0.95 0.90 475 950 25 8,550 33.3% 99.71% 5.7 C 0.85 0.98 425 190 75 9,310 69.1% 99.20% 2.5

Worked (A): TP = 0.99×500 = 495; FN = 5; FP = 0.30×9,500 = 2,850; PPV = 495/(495+2,850); NPV = 6,650/6,655.

Assistant (i): choose A. The pathologist reads every slide anyway, so a false positive costs a few seconds of extra review, while a false negative is a missed metastasis. Sensitivity dominates.

Rule-out (ii): the model-negative slides are seen by no human, so the FN count is the harm: A = 5, B = 25, C = 75 missed metastases/year. Workload removed: A 6,650 (66.5%), B 8,550 (85.5%), C 9,310 (93.1%). Choose A or B depending on the explicitly accepted miss rate; C is only defensible if local validation shows a clinically acceptable NPV and the lab accepts ~75 unseen metastases/year.

Why AUROC is useless here. AUROC integrates over all thresholds and is prevalence-independent; it does not tell you the FP/FN trade-off at a specific operating point, which is the entire decision. The threshold is a clinical risk decision: the clinical lead/pathologist with lab management and quality/regulatory sign-off, not the vendor or IT.

docs.title: Case 4 — The CE mark is not the end of the story
docs.text:
PD-L1 TPS, cut-offs 1% and 50%; vendor: 3 centres, 600 cases, ICC 0.90. Your lab: different antibody (SP263 vs 22C3), stainer, scanner, and cytology cell blocks.

Inside intended use? Antibody, stainer, scanner and specimen type all differ. Some differences may be covered by the vendor's validation; cytology cell blocks likely are not. Anything outside the intended use is your validation responsibility, and off-label use is the lab's liability.

Why ICC 0.90 is the wrong metric. ICC measures agreement on the continuous score across all values; it can be high while agreement at the clinically decisive cut-offs (1%, 50%) is poor. What matters is categorical agreement at the thresholds: accuracy/agreement, kappa, sensitivity/specificity for "≥1%" and "≥50%", with confidence intervals, plus a Bland–Altman plot focused near the cut-offs.

Site validation. ≥60 consecutive routine cases per application (CAP/ASCP/API 2022), enriched near the cut-offs, including cytology cell blocks. Reference standard: consensus of ≥3 pathologists (adjudication), not a single sign-out. Metrics: categorical agreement at 1% and 50% with CIs, plus directional bias. Pre-specify acceptance (e.g. lower CI bound of agreement ≥90%, no systematic shift).

Ground truth. There is no perfect truth near the cut-offs. Build a consensus panel with adjudication, blinded to AI, and where available use clinical outcome/response as an anchor. Report disagreement explicitly rather than pretending the sign-out is truth.

docs.title: Case 5 — HER2 drift
docs.text:
Validation combined 0 and 1+ as "negative". M4: post-neoadjuvant resections 5% → 20%. M6: HER2-low therapy makes 0 vs 1+ decisive. No error was ever raised.

  1. Patients or model? Both are plausible: post-neoadjuvant residual disease genuinely has different HER2 distributions (more 0/1+), and the model may drift with a new case mix/staining. To separate: pull case mix by indication and specimen type, scanner/stainer changes, the AI score distribution within the same subgroup, pathologist–AI agreement over time, override reasons, and re-review a sample of 0/1+ cases. If the shift disappears within matched subgroups, it is patients; if not, suspect the model.
  2. What is the old validation worth? Near zero for the new decision: it never measured 0 vs 1+ discrimination, only negative vs positive. No dashboard changes because the model output and thresholds did not change — the clinical meaning of the boundary changed, which no monitoring metric watches.
  3. New validation: enrich 0/1+ cases, consensus reference standard, metric = agreement/accuracy between 0 and 1+ at the therapy decision, pre-specified acceptance; include post-neoadjuvant cases.
  4. Who is harmed: HER2-low patients misclassified 1+→0 are denied therapy; 0→1+ may be given an inappropriate option. Rough size: at 1,500 breast cancers/year, the 0 share rose ~10 points (25→35%) and 1+ fell ~8 points; if even half of that shift is misclassification, ~60–100 patients/year are affected.

docs.title: Case 6 — The model that cannot be proven wrong
docs.text:
Zero discrepancies among "not needed" cases; vendor claims NPV 100%.

  1. Why not evidence. Only cases where IHC was not ordered were audited, and the final report is produced by the same pathologist who saw the AI suggestion (anchoring). No case has a reference standard that could reveal a missed diagnosis, so true false negatives were never measured. "Zero discrepancies" means "nobody looked for a disagreement".
  2. Design. Randomise cases near the decision boundary to IHC vs no IHC (MASAI-style), or use held-out periods; sample a random fraction of "not needed" cases for IHC and compare AI-suggested vs IHC-supported diagnosis; log the AI output and the clinical action separately; pre-register a non-inferiority margin and a safety endpoint (missed clinically significant cancers).
  3. Ethics. Doing IHC on tissue already taken is minimal risk and low cost, and there is genuine equipoise near the boundary. Answer the committee with: minimal incremental risk, clinical equipoise, opt-out/waiver, independent oversight, pre-specified stopping rules, and the fact that the current "100% NPV" claim is itself an unvalidated clinical claim.

docs.title: Case 7 — Faster, cheaper, nobody disagrees
docs.text:
Chest X-ray assistant; −22% reporting time; agreement 91% → 98.6%; senior stopped using it; juniors unsure during an outage.

  1. What does 98.6% mean? Not necessarily quality. Rising agreement is consistent with automation bias (readers defer to the AI), not calibrated trust. Data that distinguish: blinded independent reads, audits on a sample including AI-error cases, accuracy before vs after deployment, override outcomes in both directions, and whether readers detect deliberately inserted AI errors.
  2. Reverse-centaur symptoms: raising the daily target 20% (speed over judgement), requiring written justification to disagree (punishes override), reporting override rate with the aim to reduce it (treats disagreement as error), making it mandatory for everyone (removes the centaur's choice). Rewrite: AI as second reader/prioritisation, no target increase, disagreement logged without justification, override rate reviewed for both directions, opt-out allowed.
  3. Interface. Show the output after the initial read or on demand, show the image with regions rather than a single number, make dismissal one click and logged. Replace "confidence 94%" with a calibrated risk statement ("no nodule detected; sensitivity for nodules ≥8 mm is X%") or a risk band validated on local data.
  4. Legal. The radiologist who overrode with documented justification is better protected: the record shows independent judgement. Following the AI is not a defence. Designing policy that punishes override therefore increases automation bias.

docs.title: Case 8 — Business case
docs.text:
1,800 cases/year; licence €25/case; IHC in 30% of cases at €60; 40% relative IHC reduction; 12 min/case at €150/h; 20% time saving; validation 0.1 FTE; integration €40,000.

  • Licence: \(1{,}800 \times 25 = €45{,}000\)/year.
  • IHC saved: \(0.30 \times 1{,}800 \times 0.40 = 216\) cases \(\times 60 = €12{,}960\)/year.
  • Time saved: \(1{,}800 \times 12/60 = 360\) h; 20% = 72 h \(\times 150 = €10{,}800\)/year.
  • Validation: 0.1 FTE — at ~€200k loaded cost ≈ €20,000/year (state the assumption).
  • Year 1: \(12{,}960 + 10{,}800 - 45{,}000 - 20{,}000 - 40{,}000 = \mathbf{-€81{,}240}\). Steady state ≈ −€41,240/year.

So it does not pay for itself on IHC and reading time alone. It only works if freed capacity is converted into something: filling the two vacancies, avoiding locum/temporary staff, or additional throughput.

Fractional and distributed benefits: minutes saved per case, turnaround improvement, consistency. The finance director's question "which cost disappears?" has only two honest answers: IHC consumables (€12,960) and avoided locum/overtime or avoided hiring. Everything else is capacity, not cash.

Who pays / captures: the lab pays the licence, integration and validation; the insurer pays the bundled tariff; urology and patients capture faster turnaround. The bundled tariff means efficiency gains do not become revenue — the lab bears the cost and the benefit is captured elsewhere. That is the core argument for a separate funding or shared-savings arrangement.

Non-financial case: two unfilled pathologist posts, three-week backlog, urology complaints, recruitment and sub-specialisation. Evidence needed: locally validated non-inferiority, measured time saving, backlog/turnaround reduction, and staff acceptance.

docs.title: Closing questions
docs.text:
• AUROC changed the decision in almost none of the cases. The cases were decided by intended use, unit of output, operating point, drift, human factors and economics.
  • The recurring risk owner is the clinical lead / responsible pathologist or radiologist, usually not in the room when the model is bought.
  • The framework question that would have prevented most problems: Q8 (how will it be used in practice?) and Q9 (what could go wrong?), asked before purchase.

docs.title: 5 · Clinical workflow integration
Subtitles
docs.text:
1. Scope, output, and intended use
  2. Triage, concurrent assistant, QC, and autonomy
  3. Operating points and workload
  4. Site-specific and prospective validation
  5. Governance, regulation, and accountability
  6. Drift, monitoring, and revalidation
  7. Human factors and automation bias
  8. Economics and who captures value

docs.title: Milestones
docs.text:
• Place a model in the real workflow and intended use.
  • Turn sensitivity/specificity into errors, PPV, NPV, and workload.
  • Match validation evidence to autonomy and deployment site.
  • Specify monitoring, revalidation, accountability, and exit.
  • Calculate a business case and name who owns each risk and benefit.

docs.title: Possible exam questions
CASE · Q1 — A slide-level melanoma model is offered for 14,000 mixed skin specimens. Which cases are in scope, what is missing from its output, and what blocks routine use?
CASE · Q2 — Which of worklist triage, in-viewer overlay, and benign fast-track fit an adjunct intended use? How should slide scores become patient decisions?
CASE · Q3 — For 10,000 slides and 5% prevalence, calculate TP/FP/FN, PPV, NPV, and flags/day at each threshold. Which point fits assistant versus rule-out?
CASE · Q4 — A CE-IVD PD-L1 model changes antibody, stainer, scanner, and specimen type. Design site validation around 1% and 50% cut-offs and define ground truth.
CASE · Q5 — Case mix changes and a new HER2-low therapy makes 0 versus 1+ clinically important. What drift checks and new validation are required?
CASE · Q6 — If “IHC not needed” cases never receive IHC, why is zero disagreement not 100% NPV? Design an ethical evaluation of the prediction paradox.
CASE · Q7 — Radiologist–AI agreement rises to 98.6%. Does that prove benefit or calibrated trust? Redesign policy and interface around automation bias.
CASE · Q8 — Using the licence, integration, IHC, and reading-time figures, does pathology AI pay for itself? Who pays, who benefits, and what non-financial case remains?
